pradeep|Chemistry|0|1|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
An **endothermic** reaction absorbs heat (ΔH positive); an **exothermic** one gives heat out
(ΔH negative). Take the four reactions in turn.
(a) CaCO₃ ⟶ CaO + CO₂ — the thermal **decomposition** of limestone ✓
Bonds are only broken here, and the reaction has to be driven in a lime kiln at about 1100 °C.
Take the heat away and it stops at once. ΔH ≈ +178 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is **endothermic**.
(b) Fe + S ⟶ FeS — direct **combination** of the elements. Once the mixture is started with a
hot rod it glows red and continues on its own heat, ΔH ≈ −100 kJ mol⁻¹. Exothermic ✗
(c) NaOH + HCl ⟶ NaCl + H₂O — **neutralisation**. The standard enthalpy of neutralisation of a
strong acid by a strong base is −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹, which is why the beaker warms. Exothermic ✗
(d) CH₄ + 2O₂ ⟶ CO₂ + 2H₂O — **combustion**, ΔH ≈ −890 kJ mol⁻¹. This is the reaction that
heats a kitchen. Exothermic ✗
A useful general rule: decompositions are usually endothermic, while combinations,
neutralisations and combustions are usually exothermic. Only (a) is a decomposition.
(The book prints option (a) as CaO + SO₂; that is a misprint for CO₂ — a carbonate cannot
release sulphur dioxide — and it does not change the answer, since the decomposition is
endothermic either way.)
∴ CaCO₃ ⟶ CaO + CO₂.

Note: the printed key gives (c). Neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is
exothermic by definition, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (a) here.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|1|Pradeep Chemistry:
Enzyme inhibitors work in two ways, and the question is whether each statement describes
them the right way round.
A **competitive** inhibitor resembles the substrate closely enough to occupy the **active
site** itself. It competes with the substrate for that site, so the inhibition can be
reversed by adding more substrate.
A **non-competitive** (allosteric) inhibitor binds at a different site, the **allosteric
site**. That binding changes the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits,
and adding more substrate does not help.
Now test the statements.
I. There are competitive and non-competitive inhibitor drugs — **true**, those are exactly
the two classes ✓
II. These can bind at the active sites and allosteric sites — **true**, between them the two
classes use both sites ✓
III. Competitive drugs are allosteric site blocking drugs — **false**. Competitive drugs block
the *active* site ✗
IV. Non-competitive drugs are active site blocking drugs — **false**. Non-competitive drugs
bind the *allosteric* site ✗
Statements III and IV are the two correct ones swapped over, which is the trap.
So only I and II are correct.
∴ option (c).

The equilibrium constant measures how far a reaction has gone when it settles:
K = [products] / [reactants]  (each raised to its stoichiometric power)
So a **large** K means the numerator dominates — mostly products. A **small** K means the
denominator dominates — mostly reactants. The rough working rule is
K > 10³  ⇒ products predominate
K < 10⁻³ ⇒ reactants predominate
10⁻³ to 10³ ⇒ appreciable amounts of both
Here K = 1.6 × 10¹², which is a thousand million times past the 10³ mark. At equilibrium the
products outnumber the reactants by roughly that factor, so the system contains **mostly
products** ✓
Two points worth keeping straight. First, 'mostly products' is not 'all products' — a trace
of reactant always remains, however large K is, so option (c)'s mirror image would be wrong
too. Second, K says nothing whatever about **how fast** equilibrium is reached: the formation
of water from H₂ and O₂ has an enormous K, yet the mixture sits unchanged for years without
a spark.
∴ mostly products.
